questions.q: How are gender roles learned, and why is housework undervalued?

answer.text: The ways boys and girls are expected to behave are largely taught by society through socialisation, not fixed by nature. From childhood, children are given different toys, clothes, tasks and freedoms according to their sex, and are encouraged towards different qualities — boys to be tough and outdoor, girls to be gentle and home-centred. Comparisons between societies show these rules are cultural, not natural.

Housework and care work — cooking, cleaning and looking after children and the elderly — is mostly done by women and girls, is usually unpaid, and is taken for granted. Yet it is hard, time-consuming and essential; many women do it in addition to paid jobs, carrying a double burden. Recognising and sharing it fairly is an important step towards gender equality.

questions.q: How do different societies raise boys and girls differently?

answer.text: From a very young age, boys and girls are often brought up in different ways, not because of nature but because of the ideas a society holds about them.

Boys may be given cars and cricket bats and encouraged to play rough games outside, while girls may be given dolls and kitchen sets and expected to stay near the home. Girls are often asked to help with housework and to behave quietly, while boys are given more freedom to roam.

These different rules teach children that certain roles and behaviours are meant for boys and others for girls, and such ideas stay with them into adult life, shaping the work they are expected to do.

answer: Thus societies raise boys and girls differently through toys, games and rules, teaching them separate roles from childhood.

questions.q: Why should housework and care work be valued?

answer.text: A great deal of work is done inside the home, cooking, cleaning, washing, fetching water and caring for children and the elderly. This work is done mostly by women and girls.
Because housework is unpaid and done within the family, it is often not counted as real work, and those who do it are not given credit or respect for it.

Yet this work is essential, for no household could run without it, and it makes it possible for others to go out to work or study. It is hard and time-consuming, and if it had to be paid for, it would cost a great deal. Recognising and sharing this work is a matter of fairness and equality.

answer: Thus housework and care work, though unpaid, are vital and demanding, and deserve to be valued and shared.
